newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton to address Warsaw crowds on NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to address Warsaw crowds on NATO entry.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton will address thousands of Warsaw people on July 10, after Poland is asked to begin NATO entry talks, the Polish president's spokesman said on Thursday.

Clinton and his Polish counterpart Aleksander Kwasniewski will speak in the capital's Castle Square during an hour-long meeting dubbed "The Day of the Eagles," in a reference to the symbols of the two countries, spokesman Antoni Styrczula said.

Three former Soviet bloc states -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- are expected to be invited during the Western defence pact's Madrid summit on July 8-9 to begin negotiations leading to their admission to NATO in 1999.

"This visit by President Clinton has enormous political significance...in that it will show appreciation of the role of the states of Central and Eastern Europe in creating global security," Styrczula told Reuters.
He said Clinton was to arrive in Warsaw in the early afternoon of July 10 and leave the next morning for Bucharest.

Unlike Poland, Romania is among NATO applicants unlikely to be admitted in the first wave, largely because of U.S. opposition, but Clinton is expected to reassure its people that their country is well placed to join in future.
The Castle Square, where Clinton will speak, is in Warsaw's Old Town, has been rebuilt since World War Two German invaders levelled the city during its tragic 1944 uprising.

Warsaw's history recalls the repeated wars and foreign domination Poland has suffered this century and which reinforce its desire for real security within the NATO pact, confirming the country's full inclusion in democratic Europe.
Poles, like Hungarians and Czechs, escaped Soviet control only with the 1989 fall of communism.

Their leaders do not hide that, while they stress good relations with democratic Russia, they seek NATO membership partly as protection against any future return to undemocratic, expansionist policies in Moscow.
Clinton's Warsaw programme includes talks with Kwasniewski, a public concert and a state banquet on Thursday evening.
Kwasniewski said last week Clinton's visit would be a signal to those in the United States who are undecided or against NATO expansion and would sway U.S. public opinion.
"Americans often understand more through symbols than through long lectures," Kwasniewski told a radio interviewer.
NATO enlargement will have to be ratified by legislators of all 16 existing members and most crucially by two thirds of the U.S. senators, some of whom have doubts.
